title: What training do private security guards need in Portugal?
description: Portugal's Law 34/2013 and Ordinance 148/2014: initial and refresher training for private security staff, the five year PSP professional card, and fines.
shortAnswer: Under Portugal's Law 34/2013, as amended and republished by Law 46/2019, private security staff must pass approved training courses and hold a professional card issued by the Directorate of the Public Security Police (PSP), valid for five years. Renewing the card requires a refresher course. Ordinance 148/2014 sets the course structure and minimum refresher hours by specialty, from 10 hours for alarm center operators to 60 hours for close protection officers.
keyTakeaways: Law 34/2013 regulates private security, and treats training of security personnel as a private security activity in its own right (Article 1(5)).
Security staff may only perform the specialties for which their professional card qualifies them (Article 18(1)); there are nine specialties in Article 17(3).
The PSP professional card is valid for five years, and renewal requires a refresher course plus a recheck of the Article 22 requirements (Article 27).

Ordinance 148/2014 sets refresher hours by specialty, for example 30 hours for a vigilante and 40 for a segurança-porteiro, and requires refresher training if the last specialty training was over five years ago.
Keeping staff who do not meet the Article 22 training requirements is a very serious offense, with fines up to EUR 44,500 for companies.
regulator: Polícia de Segurança Pública (PSP), through its National Directorate, under the Ministry of Internal Administration
appliesTo: Private security companies holding a PSP license (alvará)
Organizations running in-house self-protection security services (serviços de autoproteção)
Private security staff in all nine specialties, including airport and port screeners and stadium stewards
Security directors, security coordinators, and heads of self-protection services
Training entities, trainers, training managers, and pedagogical coordinators in the sector

sections.heading: Which law governs private security training in Portugal?

blocks.text: Law 34/2013 of May 16, 2013 (Lei n.º 34/2013, regime do exercício da atividade de segurança privada) sets the regime for private security services and self-protection services. [Law 46/2019](https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2019/07/12800/0337703415.pdf) of July 8, 2019 amended it substantially and republished the full text, which is the version this page cites. Article 1(5) states that the professional training of private security staff and security consultancy are private security activities, regulated under the law.

The detailed training rules are in [Ordinance 148/2014](https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2014/07/13700/0390003909.pdf) of July 18, 2014 (Portaria n.º 148/2014), issued under Article 25(3) of the law. Article 4 of the Ordinance gives the National Directorate of the Polícia de Segurança Pública (PSP) exclusive competence for recognizing qualifications and for assessing and certifying private security training.

Article 17(2) of the law states that the private security profession is a regulated profession, subject to a professional title. Article 17(3) lists nine specialties: vigilante (security guard), segurança-porteiro (door supervisor for venues with dancing), close protection officer, sports venue steward, events venue steward, port and airport security assistant, cash in transit guard, public transport ticket inspector, and alarm center operator.

sections.heading: What must a person have to work in private security?

blocks.text: Security staff must meet personal requirements, pass medical and psychological evaluation, and complete approved training, permanently and cumulatively. Article 22(2) applies to security staff the requirements on nationality, compulsory schooling, full civil capacity, a clean record for listed crimes, and no recent role supervising the sector.

Article 22(7) adds the specific requirements for entering and staying in the profession: minimum physical, mental, and psychological fitness, and having attended training courses under Article 25 with success, or equivalent courses recognized in another EU or EEA state. Article 23 requires cumulative medical evaluation by occupational physicians and psychological evaluation by an entity recognized by the Ordem dos Psicólogos.

Article 18(1) states that security staff "apenas pode exercer as funções previstas para as especialidades a que se encontra habilitado com cartão profissional": they may only perform the functions of the specialties for which their professional card qualifies them. Working outside one's specialty is a very serious offense under Article 59(1)(d).

sections.heading: How is private security training structured?

blocks.text: Article 25(1) divides training into initial qualification training, refresher training, and complementary training. Article 25(2) requires a theory and a practical component in a training context, with an optional component in a real work context. Under Article 25(4), only courses delivered in certified premises, by registered trainers, following the content and duration set by ordinance, count toward the Article 22(7) requirement.

items: Initial qualification: a common base module (BAS) plus a specific module for each specialty (Ordinance 148/2014, Articles 5(2) and 9). The base module covers the internal security system and legal framework, physical and electronic security, crime prevention, emergency and alarm procedures, personal searches, conflict management, and self-defense.

Refresher (atualização): maintains competences and is a requirement for issuing or renewing authorization; content must match initial training, with at least the hours in Annex II (Articles 5(3) and 7).
Complementary: training required by other legislation for particular specialties, for example the EU module for cross-border transport of euro cash under Regulation (EU) 1214/2011 (Article 8).

blocks.text: Security directors follow a separate route. Article 22(8) of the law requires a course whose content and length are fixed by ordinance, and Article 22 of Ordinance 148/2014 requires it to be delivered by a recognized higher education institution with a minimum program of 200 hours.

sections.heading: How long is the professional card valid and what does renewal require?

blocks.text: Article 27(1) of Law 34/2013 provides that the professional card is issued by the National Directorate of the PSP, valid for five years, and renewable for equal periods. Article 27(3) states that renewal requires attending a refresher course, or an equivalent course recognized in another EU state, and a new check of the Article 22 requirements and incompatibilities. Article 29 requires security staff on duty to wear the uniform and display the card visibly.

Article 7(3) of Ordinance 148/2014 makes refresher training mandatory when renewing the card and when applying for a card where the last initial or refresher training in that specialty was more than five years ago. The minimum hours in Annex II are shown below.

sections.heading: What are the penalties for training failures in private security?

blocks.text: Article 59(1) classifies as very serious offenses, among others, working in a specialty other than the one carded (point d), keeping on duty a security director, coordinator, training manager, pedagogical coordinator, trainer, or security worker who does not meet the Article 22 requirements (point j), and failing to follow the course content, duration, and trainer requirements under Article 25(3) (point l).

Under Article 59(4), legal persons are fined EUR 1,500 to 7,500 for light offenses, EUR 7,500 to 37,500 for serious offenses, and EUR 15,000 to 44,500 for very serious offenses. Under Article 59(5), individuals are fined EUR 150 to 750, EUR 300 to 1,500, and EUR 600 to 3,000 respectively. Ancillary sanctions are also available.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each specialty's module as a set of defined competences, linked to the legal requirement, the minimum hours, and the assessment that proves the competence. The card expiry and refresher evidence sit on the same record, so an operator can show the PSP which worker holds which specialty and when it was last refreshed.

faqs.q: Can a vigilante work as a door supervisor in a nightclub?
faqs.a: Not without the segurança-porteiro specialty on the professional card. Article 18(1) of Law 34/2013 limits security staff to the functions of the specialties they are carded for, and Article 59(1)(d) makes working outside them a very serious offense. A vigilante may, however, act as an alarm center operator under Article 18(11).

faqs.q: What happens if a security worker misses the refresher before the card expires?
faqs.a: The card cannot be renewed without the refresher course under Article 27(3). Ordinance 148/2014 also requires refresher training when applying for a card if the last specialty training was more than five years ago. The worker should not be rostered until a valid card is held.

faqs.q: Who can deliver private security training in Portugal?
faqs.a: Only authorized training entities, in certified premises, using registered trainers and the content and hours set by Ordinance 148/2014. Trainers must have completed 12th grade, and training managers and pedagogical coordinators must hold a higher education degree, under Article 22(4) of Law 34/2013.

faqs.q: Are qualifications from other EU countries recognized?
faqs.a: Yes. Articles 22(7)(b) and 26 provide for recognition of equivalent courses and qualifications obtained in another EU or EEA state, with the PSP's National Directorate responsible for recognition. Article 22(11) requires sufficient knowledge of Portuguese for security staff, directors, coordinators, and trainers.
